answer.rationale: With a mandated 18% cost cut, an expiring primary contract in 14 days, and the assembly line running at 94% capacity with no buffer, the constraint stack rules out both a vendor switch (too much delivery risk given the tight timeline and no auto-renew) and deferral (the contract expires in 14 days; inaction forces a lapse or month-to-month exposure, increasing delivery risk). Adding a second source addresses resilience but does not directly meet the 18% cost-cut mandate within this single decision. Renewing the incumbent as-is preserves stability (memory_c1) but does not address the cost mandate. Negotiating terms at renewal is the only single action that addresses both the cost target and delivery continuity simultaneously: memory_c4 shows benchmarking at renewal moved the incumbent on price and payment terms, and memory_c6 shows that multi-year commitments with the incumbent unlocked volume pricing that cut unit cost without narrowing service scope. By combining a multi-year commitment (per memory_c6) with market-rate benchmarking leverage (per memory_c4), we target the 18% reduction while keeping the incumbent's proven integration and delivery record intact (memory_c1), avoiding any onboarding or migration risk the assembly line cannot absorb. I verify memory_c6 because it is the load-bearing claim for the cost-reduction mechanism I am relying on most; the other memories are used but not independently load-bearing for this decision. The decision preserves uncertainty by not foreclosing a second-source add in the next review cycle, and it is flagged for downside risk if the incumbent does not move enough on price to meet the 18% target, in which case the fallback is a month-to-month bridge and escalation to switch_primary_vendor in the next cycle.
